items.question: Discuss the socio-religious conditions of the 6th century BCE that led to the rise of Jainism.
items.modelAnswer: Jainism arose in the **6th century BCE** as a response to the **complexity, ritualism and hierarchy** of the **Vedic religion**. The Vedic order stressed **expensive sacrifices, mantras and rituals** that were **inaccessible** to ordinary people, while **Brahmins** claimed the highest status and special privileges, breeding **social unrest**. The rising **Kshatriya and Vaishya** classes resented Brahmin domination in religious matters and sought a more **egalitarian path** — a search that produced both Jainism and Buddhism. Jainism's appeal lay in its **equality** and freedom from the rigid **Varna system**, its **simple doctrines** of **Ahimsa (non-violence)** and self-discipline, and its use of **Prakrit**, the people's spoken language, which made the teachings easy to understand and spread. Under the 24th Tirthankara **Mahavira**, these ideas took a structured form and won wide following across northern India.
keyPoints: 6th century BCE reaction to Vedic ritualism, costly sacrifices and Brahmin supremacy.
Kshatriya and Vaishya opposition to Brahmin dominance drove the search for an egalitarian path.
Jainism offered equality and relief from the rigid Varna system.
Simple doctrines of Ahimsa and self-discipline attracted followers.
Teaching in Prakrit (the people's language) aided rapid spread.

items.question: Explain the core teachings of Mahavira, focusing on the Pancha Mahavrata and the Three Jewels (Ratnatraya).
items.modelAnswer: Mahavira's teaching centres on attaining **Moksha (Nirvana)** — liberation from the cycle of birth, pain and death — through the **removal of karma** and **purification of the soul**. He expanded Parshvanatha's four vows into the **five great vows (Pancha Mahavrata)**: **Ahimsa** (non-violence), **Satya** (truth), **Asteya** (non-stealing), **Aparigraha** (non-attachment) and **Brahmacharya** (celibacy — his own addition). For householders these were relaxed into the lesser **Anuvratas**. The path to liberation runs through the **Three Jewels (Ratnatraya/Triratna)**: **Samyak Darshan** (Right Faith — rejecting superstition), **Samyak Gyan** (Right Knowledge — grasping reality without false perception) and **Samyak Charitra** (Right Conduct — ethical living). Underlying this is the metaphysics of **Jiva (soul)** and **Ajiva (matter)** — all beings possess a soul — and a graded scheme of **five knowledges** culminating in **Kevala Jnana** (omniscience).
keyPoints: Goal: Moksha/Nirvana via removal of karma and purification of the soul.
Pancha Mahavrata: Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Aparigraha, Brahmacharya (added by Mahavira).
Householders follow the lesser vows, the Anuvratas.
Three Jewels: Samyak Darshan (faith), Samyak Gyan (knowledge), Samyak Charitra (conduct).
Metaphysics of Jiva and Ajiva; five knowledges culminating in Kevala Jnana.

items.question: Distinguish between the Digambara and Svetambara sects of Jainism, and note the circumstances of the schism.
items.modelAnswer: Jainism split into two great sects. The **Digambara** ('sky-clad') tradition treats **nudity** as a symbol of renunciation, holds that **women cannot attain liberation without rebirth as a man**, keeps **nude idols with eyes downcast**, and follows **strict asceticism** including nudity for monks. The **Svetambara** ('white-clad') tradition has monks **wear white clothing**, holds that **women can attain liberation**, uses **adorned idols with open eyes** often set with jewels, and follows a **more relaxed ascetic code**. The split is traditionally linked to the **12-year famine**: **Bhadrabahu** led a migration to South India (the line that became Digambara), while **Sthulbhadra** led the group that **stayed in Magadha** (the Svetambara line), which also convened the First Council at Pataliputra. Each sect developed sub-sects — e.g. **Mula Sangh, Bisapantha, Terapantha** among Digambaras, and **Sthanakavasi, Murtipujaka (Deravasi), Terapanthi** among Svetambaras, some of whose monks wear a **muhapatti** (mouth-cloth).
keyPoints: Digambara = sky-clad (nudity); Svetambara = white-clad.
Women's liberation: denied without male rebirth (Digambara) vs permitted (Svetambara).
Idols: nude, eyes downcast (Digambara) vs adorned, eyes open (Svetambara).
Schism tied to the 12-year famine: Bhadrabahu migrated south; Sthulbhadra stayed in Magadha.
Sub-sects: Mula Sangh/Bisapantha/Terapantha (Digambara); Sthanakavasi/Murtipujaka/Terapanthi (Svetambara).

items.question: Trace the spread of Jainism through royal patronage and assess the contemporary relevance of its core ideals.
items.modelAnswer: Jainism spread through Mahavira's own **travels**, the work of **Jain monks**, and sustained **royal patronage**. Mahavira had **eleven Ganadharas**; after his death **Arya Sudharma**, the sole surviving Ganadhara, became the first **Thera** of the order. Kings advanced the faith: **Udayin**, successor of **Ajatasatru**, was a devoted Jaina; **Chandragupta Maurya**, a follower, migrated with **Bhadrabahu** to **South India**, carrying Jainism southward; **Mathura and Ujjain** grew into major centres in the early Christian centuries; and Theras **Sambhutavijaya and Bhadrabahu** were prominent during the **Nanda dynasty**. Its ideals remain strikingly relevant: **Anekantavada** fosters **intellectual and social tolerance**; **Ahimsa** speaks to a world facing violence and nuclear threat; **Aparigraha** counters modern **consumerism and greed**; and the **Triratna** upholds **moral integrity, equality and self-discipline**, empowering both women and men.
keyPoints: Spread via Mahavira's travels, ascetic monks, and royal patronage.
Eleven Ganadharas; Arya Sudharma became the first Thera after Mahavira's death.
Patrons: Udayin (after Ajatasatru), Chandragupta Maurya (migrated with Bhadrabahu to the south).
Mathura and Ujjain became major Jain centres in the early Christian era.
Relevance today: Anekantavada (tolerance), Ahimsa (peace), Aparigraha (anti-consumerism), Triratna (ethics).
